title: Abraham Lincoln and Edwin Stanton: Magnanimity in the Face of Scorn
summary: When Edwin M. Stanton openly mocked Abraham Lincoln as a 'gorilla,' Lincoln overlooked the personal insult and appointed him Secretary of War to preserve the Union.
keywords: Historical Dialogue 155: அண்ணாவும் லால் பகதூர் சாஸ்திரியும்: “எண்ணிக்கை பெரும்பான்மை” vs “நெறி பெரும்பான்மை”
full_text:
In 1855, in Cincinnati, Ohio, Abraham Lincoln was engaged as an associate counsel on the prominent McCormick Reaper patent case.

The lead attorney was Edwin M. Stanton, a brilliant, abrasive legal star from Pittsburgh. When Stanton caught sight of Lincoln’s tall, unpolished frontier frame and ill-fitting coat, he recoiled with aristocratic disgust. Stanton deliberately excluded Lincoln from presenting arguments, reportedly sneering behind his back: "Where did that long-armed baboon come from? Send for a real lawyer!"

Lincoln overheard the cutting insult. Though deeply wounded, he quietly pocketed the snub and studied Stanton's brilliant courtroom arguments with admiration.

Six years later, amidst the catastrophic outbreak of the American Civil War in 1861, the Union was floundering due to corruption and incompetence in the War Department. Lincoln desperately needed an administrator of unyielding discipline and logistical mastery to run the military machine.

Lincoln announced to his stunned cabinet: "I am appointing Edwin M. Stanton as Secretary of War."

Political advisers protested vehemently: "Mr. President, have you lost your mind? Stanton despised you in Cincinnati; he openly insulted you! He still calls you a country bumpkin behind your back!"

Lincoln replied with serene, unshakable gravity:
"Gentlemen, Stanton's personal opinion of me is utterly irrelevant. What matters is that he possesses the fierce integrity and organizational genius needed to save this Union. If he can organize our armies and save our republic, he may call me a gorilla every morning before breakfast!"

Stanton accepted the post. Working side-by-side through the bloodiest years of the war, Stanton was utterly converted by Lincoln’s patience, magnanimity, and moral majesty. When Lincoln breathed his last on April 15, 1865, it was Stanton who wept at his bedside and pronounced the immortal epitaph: "Now he belongs to the ages."
